attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, presented as his own view.

semantics.note: The scored part is an observation that OpenAI was evasive. The 'if I had to guess' part is a hedged guess. It is kept in the wording but not scored.

contract.note: Reading 'incredibly evasive' as executives failing to answer a direct question is an ordinary reading. The contract rightly leaves the hedged guess unscored.

evidence.note: May 2024 report, before the post: COO Lightcap was asked directly at a Bloomberg event about Sora and YouTube and gave no clear answer.
Same article. In the March 2024 WSJ interview, CTO Murati was asked about YouTube videos and said she was not sure. This came before the post.
A separate report from the same week (March 2024) confirms Murati's 'not sure' answer when asked about YouTube.

reviews.rationale: Before the July 2024 post, two senior OpenAI executives were asked directly whether Sora was trained on YouTube data. Neither gave a yes or no (March and May 2024). That meets the support condition for evasiveness. The guess that Sora was in fact trained on YouTube is hedged and not scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own list of what OpenAI would need in order to survive.

semantics.note: This is a necessary-condition claim: survival past two years 'will have to' come with record fundraising. 'I am hypothesizing' frames it as his thesis, but the commitment itself is firm ('will have to'), not stated as a probability.

contract.note: Testing co-occurrence is fair. Survival without record fundraising would refute the claim, and the contract is clear that necessity itself cannot be tested. Its readings of a record round and of a fast follow-on pace are ordinary.

evidence.note: CNBC, September 2026: OpenAI was still operating after 2026-07-29, so the survival condition is met. This is evidence of the condition, not of the outcome.
March 2025 $40B round. Citing PitchBook, CNBC calls it the largest private tech round on record, nearly three times the previous record.
February 2026 $110B round, reported as a new record less than a year later. Some tranches are conditional.
Confirms the round closed at $122B in March 2026, and reports talks on a further round.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI was operating after the two-year mark. After the post it raised a record $40B round (March 2025), then a larger record round ($110B, closed at $122B) within a year. That meets the early-resolution rule. Only co-occurrence is shown. Whether record fundraising was strictly necessary for survival cannot be tested.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement in the post.

semantics.note: 'Requiring them to be retrained' explains the 'potentially apocalyptic consequences', so the hedge covers retraining too. The drafter's 'will' modality overstates it. The text he wrote is a possibility claim.

contract.note: The contract admits the claim is hedged but still scores it, with uneven rules: it can be settled early as supported, but is contradicted only once all cases end. Policy does not score possibility language. It also narrows 'any lawsuit' to training-data cases.

evidence.note: The plaintiff's (GEMA's) own announcement of the first-instance Munich win against OpenAI. It bears on the antecedent only, and the ruling is under appeal.
Lists the remedies in GEMA v OpenAI: an injunction on reproducing the lyrics, information, and damages. No retraining from scratch is ordered.
The Anthropic settlement requires $1.5B and destruction of the pirated files, but not retraining. It is a settlement, not a ruling for the plaintiff.

reviews.rationale: He says a plaintiff win would have 'potentially apocalyptic' consequences, and the forced retraining is part of that hedged consequence. Under policy, possibility language is not scored. Even if it were, no ruling in the packet required retraining, and with no deadline nothing would be settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own estimate in the post.

semantics.note: The wording keeps his 'if I had to just choose a number, I hypothesize' hedge. The claim is a guessed estimate of what OpenAI needs, not a firm forecast of what it will raise.

contract.note: The contract rightly treats the figure as an explicitly guessed number about a need that cannot be observed, and declines to score it.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own announcement of the $40B raise in March 2025, inside the window. It fits the view that big raises were needed, but cannot show what OpenAI actually needed.

reviews.rationale: He presents the $20B figure as a chosen number and a hypothesis about what OpenAI needs 'to even stay in the game'. That is hedged, and the need cannot be observed. OpenAI raising $40B is consistent with the estimate but does not test it.
